entries.title: ICJ to rule on Rohingya genocide case against Myanmar: What’s at stake?
entries.summary: World court to issue key verdict in its first genocide ruling in more than a decade.
entries.content:
World court to issue key verdict in its first genocide ruling in more than a decade.

The top court of the United Nations is scheduled to rule on whether Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya Muslim minority in a case brought by the West African nation of The Gambia.

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Hague is to deliver its verdict on Thursday in what will be its first judgement on the merits of a genocide case in more than a decade.

Legal experts said the ruling could bear on South Africa’s ongoing case accusing Israel of genocide in Gaza, which Israel is contesting.

The Gambia accuses Myanmar of seeking to destroy the Rohingya people during a 2017 military crackdown that forced hundreds of thousands to flee. Myanmar, meanwhile, claims it was responding to attacks by fighters from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA) on police posts.

Here’s what we know:

What happened to the Rohingya in Myanmar?

Myanmar’s military began what it called clearance operations in Rakhine State in October 2016 and a far larger campaign in August 2017 after attacks on police posts by a Rohingya armed group. About 10,000 Rohingya were killed and 740,000 forced to flee to Bangladesh, the UN estimated.

UN investigators found that soldiers razed hundreds of villages, carried out mass killings and routinely raped and gang-raped Rohingya women, girls and boys. They said the sexual violence indicated genocidal intent.

The military itself has announced convictions in only two cases brought after the violence. However, in one, seven soldiers jailed for killing 10 Rohingya men and boys at Inn Din village were freed after serving less than a year of their 10-year sentences.

In 1982, long before the crackdown, Myanmar excluded the Rohingya from its 135 recognised ethnic groups, calling them immigrant Bengalis despite many families having lived in Myanmar for generations. Nearly all Rohingya have been denied citizenship since then, making them the world’s largest stateless group.

Since fighting with the military resumed in 2023, the Arakan Army, an ethnic Rakhine armed group, has taken most of the state. The Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights said in August that both forces have committed widespread and systematic abuses against the Rohingya, accusing the Arakan Army of torture, sexual violence and forced recruitment.

The UN said those abuses have driven more than 155,000 Rohingya into Bangladesh since early 2024, taking the refugee population there up to about 1.2 million.

Nearly all the refugees live in crowded camps in the Cox’s Bazar District, where they are dependent on international aid that has fallen sharply in recent years, particularly since United States President Donald Trump’s administration slashed foreign aid in 2025. Most refugees now receive smaller food rations, and many camp schools have closed. The Office of the UN High Commissioner for Refugees warned that recent arrivals often lack sufficient food, clean water and healthcare.

Why did The Gambia take Myanmar to the ICJ?

The Gambia said it brought the case after decades of persecution of the Rohingya that culminated in the 2017 operation, which it argued breached the 1948 Genocide Convention.

The Muslim-majority nation of 2.5 million people filed the case in November 2019 on behalf of the 57-member Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC). The case was led by Abubacarr Tambadou, then The Gambia’s attorney general and justice minister.

In January 2020, the court ordered Myanmar to take emergency measures to prevent genocidal acts.

Myanmar initially argued that The Gambia, which was not directly involved in the conflict, could not bring the case. But in 2022, judges ruled that it could because both countries are parties to the convention, under which all signatories are obligated to prevent and punish genocide.

Hearings on the merits of the case followed in January this year with seven states – including Canada, France and the United Kingdom – backing The Gambia.

What exactly is the ICJ being asked to decide?

The judges must decide whether Myanmar, as a state, committed genocide against the Rohingya, thereby breaching the 1948 Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide.

The ICJ passes judgements on state actions. It does not rule on the criminal guilt of individual soldiers or commanders.

Under the convention, “genocide” refers to acts such as killing and causing serious harm committed with intent to destroy, wholly or partly, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group.

Evidence that a state has committed atrocities is not enough. The court must also find they were carried out with specific intent to destroy a group. Such intent can be shown through direct statements or orders or inferred from a pattern of conduct.

The Gambia argued that genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference from Myanmar’s conduct.

Myanmar, meanwhile, said it was conducting a legitimate counterterrorism operation against Rohingya fighters, not targeting Rohingya people as a whole.

What would a genocide finding mean for the Rohingya?

A genocide finding would formally recognise the harm the Rohingya have suffered but may do little in the short term for the more than one million victims of violence and displacement, said Michael Becker, an international law professor at Trinity College Dublin and a former ICJ legal officer.

The Gambia wants the court to order Myanmar to ensure displaced Rohingya can return safely to their land, compensate them, and replace or rebuild destroyed homes and property.

Becker told Al Jazeera the court may impose those demands only partly or in general terms, leaving Myanmar to decide how to comply with them.

Such an outcome would “surely be disappointing” to those who are sceptical that the government would fulfil those demands in good faith, he said.

“Even if the ICJ were to order far-reaching forms of relief, the political conditions on the ground in Myanmar are not amenable to realising that relief anytime soon,” Becker said.

He said a finding would instead have to be used to pressure Myanmar diplomatically.

William Schabas, an international law professor at Middlesex University in the UK, said the measures that The Gambia was seeking on behalf of the Rohingya were “robust” even though they fell short of demanding citizenship, which would end their statelessness.

“Assuming Myanmar implements the conclusions, this will indeed have significant positive effects on the security, dignity and livelihoods of the Rohingya in Myanmar,” Schabas told Al Jazeera.

What could the ruling mean for future genocide cases?

The Myanmar ruling will be the first final judgement out of five genocide cases pending before the ICJ.

Becker said the outcome could clarify the court’s longstanding “only reasonable inference” test. Under it, judges infer genocidal intent from a pattern of conduct only if no other reasonable explanation fits.

He said the court’s two rulings on the Balkan wars left it unclear whether genocide could be deemed to occur alongside armed conflict, which he said was “an unduly restrictive standard”.

Thursday’s judgement could instead treat armed conflict as an alternative explanation for a party’s conduct, rather than an automatic bar to establishing genocidal intent, he said.

According to Schabas, the ruling will “have very dramatic effects” on the outcome of the other pending cases, particularly the case against Israel.

“In my opinion, the South African case against Israel is much stronger than the case of Gambia against Myanmar. If Gambia wins against Myanmar, we can be confident that South Africa will prevail over Israel,” he said.

entries.title: Far from Trump-Putin meeting, Europe to count cost of Ukraine’s defence
entries.summary: European leaders set to meet in Berlin as Kyiv faces a 25 billion-euro ($27.4bn) financing gap next year.
entries.content:
European leaders set to meet in Berlin as Kyiv faces a 25 billion-euro ($27.4bn) financing gap next year.

As US President Donald Trump shakes hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin in China, European leaders are due to gather in Berlin to agree on funding for Ukraine’s defence and press Washington’s visiting envoys for a European role in Russia-Ukraine peace talks.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is hosting the so-called Coalition of the Willing summit on Thursday alongside French President Emmanuel Macron and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham. More than 30 leaders are expected to attend, including Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

The summit agenda includes long-term security guarantees and continued military and financial support for Ukraine. Zelenskyy has said air defence will be his immediate priority as Kyiv enters a winter with the threat of Moscow’s drone attacks looming.

Trump administration envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are expected, according to media reports, to meet Ukrainian officials and Europe’s newly formed negotiating team in Berlin. The team includes France, Germany, the United Kingdom, Italy and Poland, plus European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa.

Washington has backed European participation in the next round of talks, but Moscow has yet to agree.

The impasse could put Ukraine’s main financial backer on the sidelines of talks over its future, as European Union countries are set to make even steeper commitments.

The European Commission on Wednesday proposed an additional 45 billion-euro ($49.3bn) loan for 2027, with up to 25 billion euros ($27.4bn) for military aid and 20 billion euros ($21.9bn) for budget support. That follows a 1.71 billion-euro ($1.87bn) payment on Monday under an existing EU loan for drones, ammunition and air defence.

Even if the new loan is approved, it would leave a 25 billion-euro ($27.4bn) financing gap next year.

‘Quite a stupid thing’

Zelenskyy said the US envoys had promised to brief Kyiv on Trump’s discussions in China, where he is meeting Chinese President Xi Jinping and Putin.

The Berlin summit gives European negotiators a chance to agree on what they want from the next round and put it directly to Trump’s envoys, just days after a public disagreement between the transatlantic partners emerged in Brussels.

At Tuesday’s Ukraine Defence Contact Group meeting at NATO headquarters, Elbridge Colby, the Pentagon’s undersecretary for policy, argued that some Ukrainian strikes deep inside Russia had done little to slow Moscow’s military advances and that attacks on civilian infrastructure may have hardened Russian resolve.

In a swift backlash, German Federal Minister of Defence Boris Pistorius called the assessment “quite a stupid thing” and pointed to Russia’s repeated attacks on Ukraine’s electricity and heating infrastructure. London was quick to align with Berlin, with UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting arguing that Ukraine should decide how to fight and that its long-range strikes had weakened Russia’s military capabilities.

After a nine-month hiatus, US, Ukrainian and Russian officials resumed talks in Abu Dhabi last week. Witkoff and Kushner then met Putin in Moscow and said Europeans would join the next round, despite Moscow throwing cold water on the idea.

Europe gets a seat at the table

Within Europe, newfound energy has emerged with the prospect of the bloc joining negotiations, with EU leaders agreeing in Dublin last week on a team.

Sharon Hudson-Dean, a senior fellow with the Center for European Policy Analysis, told Al Jazeera that “success” in Berlin would mean firmer commitments to Ukraine’s immediate defence and its 2027 budget, as well as closer alignment between Washington and European capitals.

European leaders, she said, are wary of US announcements and Russian intentions and want a say in decisions that will affect their security, budgets and markets.

“Washington should leave Berlin recognising that Europe will shoulder much of the financial and security burden of implementing any settlement, and as such, needs a seat at the table,” Hudson-Dean said.

With Europeans likely to bear many of the costs of security guarantees, sanctions and Ukraine’s path to EU membership, she said, they want to be “in on the takeoffs, not just the crash landings”.

Ahead of the Berlin summit, European allies pledged more winter aid for Kyiv and outlined plans to deliver fighter jets and air defence missiles, as Zelenskyy urged them to release Patriot and IRIS-T interceptors from their stocks, offering to replace them with missiles Kyiv has on order.

The Ukrainian leader also said Ukraine needed 40 more F-16s.

In response, Germany and Norway each announced $300m for the Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL), a NATO-coordinated programme that buys US weapons for Ukraine. Their joint package includes Patriot missiles.

The UK, Denmark, the Netherlands, Finland, Belgium, France, Sweden, Lithuania, Estonia and Portugal all reiterated or pledged further funding for Ukraine in the lead-up to the Berlin summit.

European rifts

Poland will be represented on Europe’s negotiating team, but Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Friday that Warsaw would put no additional money into PURL at this stage. Bulgaria, Hungary, the Czech Republic and Slovakia have indicated they will opt out of the next round of EU financing.

Despite elections in Hungary that ushered in a more EU-friendly leadership, Budapest continues to oppose military assistance for Kyiv.

Kinga Koranyi, an assistant professor at the University of Wroclaw who studies Hungarian politics and EU governance, told Al Jazeera the idea that Hungary should “stay out of the war” remains widely shared after years of politicisation under former Prime Minister Viktor Orban’s Fidesz party, leaving direct funding for Kyiv unpopular.

Years of lost access to EU funds over rule-of-law disputes have also made Budapest cautious about new spending, she said, as the cost of the war with no end in sight continues to mount.

entries.title: Trump makes third Supreme Court bid to end Venezuelan migrant protections
entries.summary: Emergency appeal follows a California judge's ruling that ending their temporary protected status was unlawful.
entries.content:
Emergency appeal follows a California judge’s ruling that ending their temporary protected status was unlawful.

US President Donald Trump’s administration has asked the Supreme Court to issue an emergency order allowing officials to strip legal protections for hundreds of thousands of Venezuelan migrants, marking the third time it has appealed to the nation’s top judicial body over the issue.

The Department of Justice on Wednesday filed an emergency application asking the Supreme Court to put on hold a federal judge’s ruling that officials lacked the authority to end the Temporary Protected Status (TPS) granted to the migrants under former President Joe Biden.

San Francisco-based US District Judge Edward Chen’s ruling is due to take effect on Friday unless a federal appeals court or the Supreme Court moves to suspend it. The Supreme Court previously paused Chen’s ruling in October 2025.

The Trump administration argued that reinstating TPS for Venezuelans would prevent the administration from carrying out up to 332 removal orders and require it to provide them with work authorisation. It also argued that reinstating the protections would cause “severe and immediate harm”.

If the justices do not intervene again before Friday, the administration could be required to release about 1,800 Venezuelans from detention, federal attorneys wrote.

The plaintiffs who challenged the administration’s actions, including TPS holders and an advocacy group, said that since the previous Supreme Court intervention in the case, Venezuelan TPS holders have been detained, separated from children who are US citizens, deported to Venezuela, and even sent to so-called “third countries” where they have no ties.

The Supreme Court in June backed the administration’s separate actions ending TPS for hundreds of thousands of Haitians and Syrians, giving a boost to the Republican president’s hardline approach towards immigration.

Trump clamps down on TPS

TPS is a designation that lets migrants from countries stricken by war, natural disaster or other catastrophes live and work in the US while it is unsafe for them to return to their home countries.

A person granted TPS cannot be deported, can obtain an employment authorisation document, and may be given travel authorisation. A TPS holder cannot be detained by the US over their immigration status.

The Trump administration has terminated TPS for more than 1 million people from 13 countries, including Venezuela, Haiti, Honduras, Nicaragua, Afghanistan and Syria. But in a change in practice, the administration kept protections in place for nearly 200,000 Salvadorans whose TPS was set to expire by September 9, and for more than 100,000 people from Ukraine and Sudan in October.

Millions of people have fled Venezuela in recent years due to political repression and a crippling economic crisis spurred in part by US sanctions against the government of President Nicolas Maduro.

Before leaving office, the Biden administration had extended TPS for about 600,000 Venezuelans through October 2026.

The State Department currently warns people to reconsider travel to Venezuela due to the risk of crime, kidnapping and poor health infrastructure, among other issues.

entries.title: Elon Musk says he feels ‘pretty foolish’ about US midterm spending
entries.summary: Musk says campaign cash alone cannot decide elections, even as he heavily funded Republican candidates in Texas.
entries.content:
Musk says campaign cash alone cannot decide elections, even as he heavily funded Republican candidates in Texas.

Elon Musk has said he feels “pretty foolish” about the amount of money he spent on this year’s US midterm elections after Republicans suffered sweeping losses.

Speaking virtually at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX and the world’s richest man said: “I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money, and not seeing much for it.”

He added that Republican candidates might have fared worse without his spending, but that the outcome showed campaign cash alone could not decide an election.

“Probably, if I could rewind the clock, I would have spent less money,” he said.

Musk spent nearly half a billion dollars to back Republican candidates and keep Texas – home to Tesla, SpaceX, and a planned chipmaking venture between the two companies – under Republican control, according to the Reuters news agency.

Democrats won both chambers of Congress, and Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated Republican Governor Greg Abbott in Texas, a rebuke to President Donald Trump, a close Musk ally.

Musk’s biggest focus was the Texas Senate race, where Republican Ken Paxton lost to Democrat James Talarico.

‘I’m not MAGA’

Musk also sought to distance himself from the Republican Party’s base, The New York Times reported. “I’m not MAGA,” he said, referring to Trump’s Make America Great Again movement. “If that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don’t have that.”

He has previously described himself as MAGA, and even “dark gothic MAGA”, The New York Times said. “There are positives and negatives in both parties,” Musk said, and conceded that his effort “failed, by the way, obviously”.

He predicted that policy in Texas would be “fine” under Hinojosa, whom he called “quite moderate” and “not a far-left governor”.

Hinojosa supports keeping a moratorium on new data centres in the state, according to The New York Times.

Anthropic and SpaceX

On his artificial intelligence plans, Musk said the AI company Anthropic was “extremely likely” to continue renting computing capacity from SpaceX, and wanted significantly more.

He said the most likely outcome was that Anthropic would ask for an additional 10 gigawatts, according to a recent Reuters report.

entries.title: Miami court convicts US-Haitian pastor over 2021 assassination of president
entries.summary: Prosecutors accused Christian Emmanuel Sanon of seeking to replace then-Haitian President Moise.
entries.content:
Prosecutors accused Christian Emmanuel Sanon of seeking to replace then-Haitian president Moise.

A Florida pastor with dual Haitian-American citizenship has been convicted in the United States on charges stemming from the assassination of Haitian President Jovenel Moise, following a nearly eight-week trial in a federal court in Miami.

Christian Emmanuel Sanon, 68, was found guilty on Wednesday on all eight charges, including conspiring to kill the Caribbean nation’s president, who was shot dead in his home on July 7, 2021.

Prosecutors said in court records that the scheme to kill Moise, 53, included paying about two dozen foreign mercenaries with money obtained from US government programmes that were intended to help businesses during the COVID-19 pandemic.

They said South Florida was a hub for planning and financing the plot to oust Moise and install a president of the conspirators’ choosing.

Sanon acknowledged in trial testimony that he was in communication at one point with people trying to replace Moise, but said the group had moved on to another candidate long before the assassination. He denied any knowledge of plans to kill the president and maintained his innocence throughout the trial.

He was arrested in Haiti’s capital, Port-au-Prince, days after the assassination. According to a report by local police seen by the Reuters news agency, when officers searched his residence, they found eight vehicle registration plates, 19 passports and 12 mobile phones, as well as 30 boxes of ammunition and 12 pistol holsters.

Widow turned presidential candidate

Moise’s widow, Martine Moise – a key witness in the trial – was flown to Florida for treatment for bullet wounds she sustained in the attack. She has now registered as a presidential candidate for Haiti’s 2027 general election, the first in more than 10 years.

Sanon, who remains in federal custody, showed little reaction as the jury verdict was announced. He faces up to life in prison and is set to be sentenced on February 10.

His attorney, Zeljka Bozanic, said the defence team was disappointed and would file an appeal at the appropriate time. Prosecutors declined to comment after the verdict.

US prosecutors have charged more than 40 people with crimes related to the assassination, and a dozen have been convicted, including five who are serving life sentences.

A new list of indictments released by US prosecutors in September included four people whose names were redacted.

Seven more people have been charged for their roles in facilitating the funding of the assassination plot and helping those responsible evade justice after the killing, including Vitel’homme Innocent, a gang leader tied to the kidnapping of 17 US and Canadian missionaries later in 2021. He has yet to be arrested.

Those still to face trial include Joseph Felix Badio, a former government anti-corruption official whom other suspects’ defence lawyers have accused of masterminding the operation, and 17 Colombian former soldiers flown in from Haiti in September.

Assassination plunges Haiti into turmoil

Haiti has not had a president since authorities said a squad of mostly retired Colombian soldiers impersonating US Drug Enforcement Administration agents killed Moise and injured his wife in a night-time raid on their home outside Port-au-Prince.

A series of transitional governments followed, as armed gangs, widely believed to be aided by corrupt politicians, seized control of much of the capital and surrounding regions.

The United Nations Human Rights Office documented 4,595 people killed in armed violence between January 1 and October 31 this year.

The situation has caused economic, security and humanitarian crises, forcing nearly 1.5 million people to flee their homes, according to the UN.
